scribe_response.text: Tell me about a time you moved to a new place. The biggest, biggest move of my life was in nineteen seventy-nine, when I flew from Kochi to Abu Dhabi. I was um twenty-seven, and I had never been on an aeroplane before. My mother packed a tin of banana chips and a small bottle of coconut oil in my bag. At the airport my father held my hand a little too long, and said nothing at all. The flight was long, and I pressed my um forehead to the window whenever the lights of a town went by. When the door opened at Abu Dhabi, the heat struck me like the opening of a furnace. It was August, and the air was so humid that my spectacles fogged instantly. A driver from the company met me with a card that spelled my name wrongly. We drove along a road that was almost empty, with sand on either side and the sea shining ahead. I um remember that the uh city was small then, with low white buildings and a great many cranes. The company gave me a uh room in a shared house near the plant, with four other bachelors. We had one refrigerator, one television, and a rule that nobody cooked fish on um weekdays. My roommates were from Kerala, Punjab, and Sri Lanka, and we ate together in the evenings. What happened next? I learned to make dal and chapati from a Punjabi engineer named Harbans, who treated cooking as a science. Harbans kept a jar of green chillies on the windowsill and guarded it jealously. The plant itself stood on the coast, and its job was to turn seawater into drinking water. I found that astonishing, because I had grown up with so much rain that, rain that I never thought about thirst. Here every drop was counted, and nobody wasted a glass. The first months were lonely, and I wrote a letter home every Sunday on thin blue paper. Letters took ten days each way, and I read the replies until the folds went soft. My mother wrote about the mango tree, and my father wrote about the school. Sometimes I stood at the window at night and tried to imagine the courtyard and the tulsi plant. Slowly the city welcomed me, because the people were generous and the shopkeepers were patient. A Lebanese baker near our house gave me warm bread every morning and refused to take money on Fridays. On my uh first payday I bought a small radio and tuned it to Malayalam songs. The shortwave signal came and went, but I loved it. Can you tell me more about that? That little radio sat on my shelf for twenty years. I learned a few words of Arabic, enough to bargain and to thank people. On weekends we drove to the corniche, and the sea breeze felt like a cool hand on the forehead. After two years, my family arranged my marriage, and Lakshmi came to join me in a small flat. She found the first winter harder than I had, because um she missed her sisters. We bought a small stove and a pressure cooker, and the flat began to smell like home. Our sons were born in that country, Arun first and then Vivek, and they grew up with two homes. I never planned to stay for my entire career, and yet I did. Each year I told myself that I would return to Kerala, and each year the plant needed me. Moving was hard, but it widened me, and I do not regret uh it. A person can plant roots in two places if he waters both carefully. Now my sons say that Abu Dhabi is their home, and I understand them perfectly. When I visit Thrissur, people call me the Gulf man, and I smile. I am a man of two courtyards, one of red clay and one of white stone.
